newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU dilutes measures to save fish stocks.
newsitem.headline: EU dilutes measures to save fish stocks.

text.p: A European Union agreement this week to reduce fishing over the next five years to save endangered stocks has been substantially toned down following strong pressure from fishermen fearful for their jobs.
The deal, struck by EU fisheries ministers in Luxembourg on Tuesday, foresees reductions in catches of depleted and overfished stocks of 30 percent and 20 percent respectively by the end of 2001.
The European Commission, citing scientific advice, had fought for cuts of 40 percent and 30 percent over six years for North Sea cod, herring, mackerel and other threatened species.
But the final cutbacks, contained in a Dutch EU presidency compromise, were still too much for Britain and France to swallow.
Britain insisted that the problem of Spanish and Dutch "quota-hoppers" be tackled first.

"We are not prepared to continue to see a situation where over a quarter of the British fishing fleet is foreign-owned and foreign-controlled," British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry told reporters after being outvoted.
Quota-hopping is the practice whereby foreign trawlermen have legally set up flag-of-convenience operations in England to buy licences that give them access to British fishing quotas.

France said the curbs were still too sharp despite a halving of the rates proposed by the Commission last year. "Reduction rates remained too high," French Fisheries Minister Philippe Vasseur said in a statement. France had earlier called for cuts of only 15 percent over three years.
Diplomats noted that France is facing legislative elections in a year's time when fishing industry votes could prove vital in certain regions, such as Brittany.

Baldry, battling for fishermen's votes for the Conservative party in elections on May 1, said that Britain would not implement further fishing reductions until the "quota hopper" problem had been resolved.
"The UK can well meet that (30 percent) target by eliminating quota-hoppers from our register, and that we are determined to do," he added.
But Dutch Fisheries Minister Jozias Van Aartsen said that Britain had scarcely raised the quota hopping issue during two days of ministerial talks.
"I haven't heard anything about quota hopping today," Van Aartsen told a news conference after the meeting.
He stressed that the fisheries reduction programme must be implemented by all member states.
EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino said that quota hopping was a separate issue and she hoped that Britain would respect EU law.

"I grew up convinced that the U.K. was a state which abided by the law...I also grew up thinking that the U.K. was very much committed to free trade and the free movement of capital," she told the news conference.
"Everybody has to abide by the law," Bonino stressed, adding that detailed national fishing reduction programmes will be drawn up by June 30, 1996.

EU officials said Tuesday's deal, which also resolved Swedish concern over a Baltic cod fishing cutback, would free hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to restructure Europe's fishing industry. The aid goes mainly to southern member states and Ireland.
